The Belgian DPA reaffirmed the standard conditions for minimization of data (Article 5(1)(c) GDPR) in relation with the lawfulness of the data processing (Article 6 GDPR) and underlines that a data subject's request for erasure of their personal data pursuant to Article 17 GPDR must be granted if the data processing is not lawful to begin with.
The Austrian DPA held that the GDPR does not apply to the expulsion of an individual from a religious organisation.

The Irish DPC conducted an own-volition inquiry into Irish Credit Bureau DAC after a personal data breach in which 1,062 inaccurate accounts were shared with credit bureau members and data subjects following database coding changes. It found infringements of Articles 25(1), 5(2) and 24(1) GDPR, issued a reprimand, and imposed a fine only for the Article 25(1) infringement. The fine was set at EUR 220,000 before mitigation, reduced by EUR 130,000 for mitigating factors, giving EUR 90,000. No fine was imposed for the Articles 5(2) and 24(1) infringement.

The Swedish DPA (Integritetsskyddsmyndigheten) issued a reprimand on Rebtel Networks AB for violating Article 17 GDPR by not deleting personal data of the complainant without undue delay and Article 23 GDPR by providing incorrect information about deletion of personal data.
The Slovenian DPA decided that covert video surveillance of employees is not permissible in any manner or under any circumstances.
The Polish DPA (UODO) imposed a fine of €5000 on a company for failing to cooperate with the DPA in the investigation of a complaint about irregularities in the processing of personal data.

The Slovenian DPA decided that it is permissible for an individual to disclose to a third party the blog author's specific health information. Information whose content meets the definition of health data in point 15 of Article 4 GDPR is health information even if it is published by the person himself.

The Slovenian DPA stated that obtaining information on the child's health and developmental characteristics, knowledge of which is necessary for the child's safety and work with the child, and on whether the child has been vaccinated, is not appropriate at the stage of submitting an application for enrollment in kindergarten.

The Icelandic DPA held that the Reykjavík Health Inspectorate had a right to enter and take photos of the complainant's property while enforcing the Icelandic laws on hygiene and pollution prevention.
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) fined an audit company €3,000 for a security breach occurred when they sent the claimant information of another client, instead of theirs.
The Slovenian DPA (IP) stated that, when courts process personal data as an judicial authority, the IP is not competent under Article 55(3) GDPR.

The Belgian DPA (APD/GBA) ordered the defendant (a public institution) to comply with the principles of purpose limitation and data minimization, by removing the mention of the title of nobility from the identity card of the complainant.

The Bavarian DPA ("Bayrisches Landesamt für Datenschutzaufsicht" - BayLDA) held that the use of the newsletter tool Mailchimp by a German company was unlawful as Mailchimp receives email adresses of newsletter subscribers and might qualify as an "electronic communication service provider" under US surveillance law.
The AEPD fined €3,000 a Cultural Association for sharing in WeChat pictures of the minor child of the complainant without their consent.

Teachers at two lower secondary schools in Ålesund required pupils to download the Strava training app onto their private phones for PE lessons, and used its tracking function to check task completion. The municipality notified a personal data breach to Datatilsynet on 5 May 2020. Datatilsynet found that the municipality had no risk assessment, no DPIA and no routines for approving apps, and fined it NOK 50,000 for infringements of Articles 32(1)(b) with Article 5, 24(1) and 35 GDPR. The decision stresses that the problem was the municipality's app procedures, not Strava itself.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) fined Air Europa Líneas Aéreas S.A. €600,000 for the infringement of Articles 32(1) and 33 GDPR, due to the lack of appropriate technical and organisational measures and of an adequate level of security and due to the delay in the notification of a personal data breach.

Asker municipality published its mailing lists (postlister) on its website with document titles containing national ID numbers and confidential information, including about children (special education, PPT decisions, housing grants), over about 16 years. A private person alerted the municipality, which notified the Datatilsynet. The authority found there was no legal basis for publication, inadequate security ensuring confidentiality and inadequate routines for handling the lists. It imposed an administrative fine of NOK 1,000,000.

The Slovenian DPA held that the Ministry of Public Administration did not provide the relevant information under Article 13 GDPR when processing expressions of interest for COVID-19 vaccination on the e-government portal.
The Slovenian DPA stated that, according to the Slovenian Personal Data Protection Act, a public body could not link two medical registries without the DPA's prior permission.

The Slovenian DPA decided that personal data collected when registering an interest in vaccination through the e-government portal may only be processed after the individual has received clear, accurate and reliable information about who is collecting it and for what purpose.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) fined Vodafone €100,000 (reduced to €60,000 for voluntary payment and acknowledgement of responsibility) for repeatedly processing of personal data of a data subject that had opposed the processing.
The Icelandic DPA reprimanded a hospital for sending medical data of a complainant and her child to the wrong address.

A complainant asked the municipality of San Marco in Lamis to remove from its website two mayoral orders containing his and his family members' personal data (birth date and place, tax code, residence), linked to an unauthorised building works case. The municipality refused, and the data stayed online for more than three years, beyond the 15-day period for the public notice board, and were reachable through an archive page found by search engines. The Garante found breaches of the data minimisation principle, of the lack of a legal basis for publication beyond 15 days, and of the related GDPR principles, and imposed a fine of EUR 3,000 plus publication of the decision on its website.

The Dutch DPA received a complaint in July 2018 about sensors in Enschede's city centre that picked up the wifi signals of passers-by's phones. The investigation found that eleven sensors collected pseudonymised MAC addresses, signal strength, date and time from hundreds of thousands of people between 25 May 2018 and 30 April 2020. The municipality had no legal basis for this processing, so it breached Article 5(1)(a) in conjunction with Article 6(1) GDPR. The AP fined the municipality EUR 600,000, raising the EUR 525,000 base amount by EUR 75,000 because of the seriousness and the municipality's culpability.

The Italian DPA investigated call centre Mediacom after hundreds of complaints about unwanted telemarketing calls made for TIM. Between 2016 and 2019 Mediacom called 15,410 'referenced' numbers outside the contact lists, 11,232 of them for TIM, with no valid consent or other legal basis. The consent on the purchased lists was not specific or free, and only a sample of the lists was checked. The Garante found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a) and 6(1), permanently restricted the processing, ordered compliance and imposed a fine of EUR 15,000, taking into account Mediacom's financial crisis after losing the TIM contract, and ordered publication of the decision.

After hundreds of complaints about unwanted promotional calls made on behalf of TIM, the Garante inspected the call centre Planet Group. It found the company called 47,981 'referenced' numbers outside TIM's lists without a legal basis or consent, kept calling people who had objected, called some people very insistently, and had inadequate privacy-by-design. The Garante treated Planet Group as de facto (joint) controller, imposed a permanent limitation of the processing with compliance orders, and fined it EUR 80,000, with publication of the decision.

The Baden-Württemberg data protection commissioner closed proceedings against VfB Stuttgart 1893 AG and imposed a fine of EUR 300,000 for negligent breach of the accountability obligation under Art. 5(2) GDPR. The club and its parent association cooperated extensively with the investigation. Besides the fine, the company restructured its data protection management and will support youth data protection awareness projects. Some publicly discussed matters could not be fully examined because of limitation rules. This is a press release, not the full fine notice.

The Spanish Data Protection Authority (AEPD) fined Filigrana Comunicación with €8,000 for the infringement of Articles 6(1), 13 and 14 GDPR, as the company gathered and re-used data from the Andalusian Education Department without a legitimate basis, and they did not fulfill their information obligations.
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) imposed a fine of €50,000 to EQUIFAX IBERICA, S.L. for including the personal data of the claimant in its solvency file without legal basis for it.
The Icelandic DPA ruled that the processing of personal information by a financial institution in connection with cash transactions was permitted on the basis of the Icelandic money laundering law.
The Icelandic DPA ordered an operator of a sale website to stop the processing of users' personal data. According to the DPA, the consent was not sufficiently informed.

The Icelandic DPA held that a controller was not permitted to disclose personal information about the complainant from a non-conclusive judgment to a credit rating company. Additionally, the credit rating company was not permitted to process information on the complainant's claim in its default register.

The Icelandic DPA held that the chief of police in the capital area has not complied with the Law on the processing of personal data for law enforcement purposes when requesting information and suggestions via Facebook.

Dragefossen AS, an energy company, operated a panning webcam on its office roof that live-streamed Rognan town centre on YouTube and its website, with up to 12 hours of rewind. Although faces and number plates were not legible, people could be identified from clothing, car type and other features, so personal data was processed. The company had not identified any legal basis, and the authority found none under Article 6(1)(f). It fined the company NOK 150,000 for infringing Articles 6(1) and 5(1)(a). The order to stop the surveillance was dropped because the camera had already been switched off.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) imposed a fine of €150,000 on Xfera Móviles S.A. (defendant) for infringing Article 17, 32, 5(1)(f) GDPR and Article 21 LSSI. The fine was imposed after investigating two complaints received from the same data subject who indicated that the defendant had not stopped sending marketing messages and that the data subject was able to access third party's personal data through the 'Mi Yoigo' platform.

The Cypriot DPA imposed a reprimand and a warning on a professional association for having unlawfully processed the personal data of one of its former members, and for failing to cooperate with the DPA in the course of the complaint procedure.

The Romanian DPA (ANSPDCP) imposed a fine of €500 on a natural person who held the office of Secretary-General in a subsidiary branch of a political party in the City of Bucharest for publishing the personal data of 10 individuals on their website. This breached Articles 5(1)(f) and 32 GDPR.

An employer asked an employee to set up automatic forwarding of their email to a shared mailbox, for operational reasons. After a complaint, the Norwegian DPA found there was no legal basis for the forwarding, in breach of the email-access regulation and the GDPR requirement of a legal basis. The enterprise also had no routines for access to email. It was ordered to improve its internal control and guidelines and to pay NOK 250,000.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) imposed a fine of €200,000 on the energy supplier, I-DE, Redes Eléctricas Inteligentes SAU. I-DE had sent a letter to end consumers requiring them to get in touch with regards to unpaid invoices despite a contractual arrangement providing for an intermediary to communicate with end users (breach of Articles 6(1)(b), 5(1)(b) and 5(1)(c) GDPR).

The ICO held that a recruitment consultancy contravened Article 15 GDPR for failing to comply with the data subject's access request under Article 15 GDPR, as the company could not evidence its claim that the Employment Tribunal instructed them not to provide any documentation.

The UK DPA (ICO) fined Leads Work Limited approximately €288,000 for sending unsolicitated direct marketing communication to individual subscribers, in breach of Regulation 22 of the PECR. The ICO considered the GDPR's definition of consent.

The ICO (International Commissioner's Officer) has fined Leads Works Ltd 250000 GBP (€291,237) for sending more than 2.6 million nuisance and unlawful direct marketing text messages to customers without their valid consent. Leads Works Ltd has continued to send significant numbers of marketing texts to individuals throughout, and since, the course of the Commissioner's investigation, incurring a substantial amount of complaints.

The Icelandic DPA ruled in a case regarding the use of audio and video recording equipment in police cars by the police in the capital area in 2017 and 2018. The decision finds that the complainant's right to information, including the police's obligation to provide information, was respected in 2017 but not in 2018.

The Slovenian DPA decided that there is no legal basis for conducting a method of distance learning that uses untested facial recognition technologies or software that allows control over individual behavior. It is also not permissible to require an individual (student) to record the entire room in which the exam is being written. In these cases (it is) an excessive intrusion into the privacy of the individual, as the review and assessment of knowledge could certainly be enabled in a way that is less intrusive into the privacy of the student.

The Spanish Data Protection Agency (AEDP) imposed a warning sanction on a local council for using a biometric control system to monitor the working hours of employees without having informed them in accordance with Article 13 GDPR.
The Italian DPA (Garante per la protezione dei dati personali) imposed a fine of €300,000 on the national social security institute (INPS) for violating Articles 5(1)(a)(c)(d), 2, 25 and 35 GDPR.

A former employee of the Comune di Conflenti complained that a municipal council resolution published on the online notice board (Albo Pretorio) named her and contained employment information, including an extract of her resignation letter. The Garante found the publication unlawful: there was no valid legal basis for disseminating the data, the data were minimised incorrectly, and the resolution stayed online beyond the period set by the transparency rules. The municipality was fined EUR 2,000, which the Garante said was effective, proportionate and dissuasive. The Garante also ordered publication of the decision on its website, but no further corrective measures, because the municipality had removed the data and the processing had ended.

A former employee complained that the municipality of Commezzadura published on its online notice board a decision accepting his resignation. It included assessments of his work and information on his sick leave, identifying him by initials. The mayor also gave the press details that appeared in a newspaper. The Garante found no legal basis for the publication, and health data may never be disseminated. It fined the municipality EUR 6,000 and ordered publication of the decision on its website.

On 25 October 2019 the website repubblica.it, linked to Gedi, published images of two people detained over a serious crime, shown visibly physically restrained (handcuffs only pixelated). The Garante urgently restricted further dissemination, but Gedi neither replied nor removed the images until 25 February 2020, and similar images were still online on 18 February 2021. The Garante found the publication unlawful and contrary to Article 5(1)(a) GDPR, the Italian Code and the journalists' code of ethics, and found non-compliance with its order and its information request. It banned further processing of such images, fined Gedi EUR 20,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

A parent complained that the Regional School Office for Lazio, answering a request from the Public Administration Department about alleged irregularities in the allocation of support teaching hours, sent documents containing his child's personal and health data, including a diagnostic code. The Garante found that the disclosure was not necessary to answer the Department and had no suitable legal basis, so it breached Articles 5(1)(a), 6 and 9 GDPR and Articles 2-ter and 2-sexies of the Italian Code. It fined the office EUR 4,000 and ordered publication of the decision on its website.

A university hospital in Florence notified a personal data breach: paper health documentation (an emergency room lab report) of one patient was handed to another person, caused by a doctor picking up a printout left in a shared printer tray. The Garante found unlawful communication of health data in breach of Articles 5 and 9 GDPR. It considered no further corrective measures necessary because the conduct had ceased and improvements were made, but imposed a fine of EUR 6,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) imposed a fine on Avilon Center SL for making a commercial call to a individual registered on the Robinson List in breach of Article 48(1)(b) LGT and Article 21 GDPR in conjunction with Article 23(4) LOPDGDD. Avilon Center SL made an voluntary, early and guilty payment of €12,000.

The Austrian DPA ordered the controller to provide the data subject with the complete personal data of her medical history within a period of four weeks for a violation of Article 15 GDPR, since the controller withheld personal data from the data subject to which she had a right.

The Croatian DPA (AZOP) found that the leading security company in Croatia, acting as a data processor, enabled the data breach by not maintaining adequate and sufficient technical and organizational measures for personal data security for more than two and a half years.

The Spanish Data Protection Agency (AEPD) imposed a warning sanction on a private individual for the installation of a video surveillance system without informing the subjects who may be recorded of the data processing, in violation of Article 13 and Article 5 (1) (c) GDPR.

The Icelandic DPA held that the processing of personal data by a municipality regarding reimbursement of foreign medical expenses was necessary to fulfill the legal obligation that rests on the institution.

The ICO (International Commissioner's Officer) has fined the Valca Vehicle Ltd 80,000 GBP (€92,718) for sending more than 95,000 nuisance, marketing messages during the pandemic from June to July 2020 without the recipients’ permission.
The Finnish DPA ordered Suomen Asiakastieto Oy to remove a payment default entry from their credit information registry which no longer had a legal basis to be be retained.
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) sanctioned a city hall for not satisfying a data subject's access request to his personal data concerning the payment of local taxes.

The Belgian DPA (APD/GBA) assessed whether the defendant (an autonomous provincial public entity for tourism) breached the GDPR by placing intelligent cameras to count passer-by at specific locations during the Covid-19 pandemic. The DPA assessed the legal basis for this processing and whether the principles of privacy by design and by default provided data subjects with transparent information concerning this processing.

A customer complained that a sports retailer sent him promotional SMS messages after he had objected by email to receiving marketing. The company said his number had been deleted, but a second promotional SMS arrived in November 2019 because of an employee's error. The Authority found that the company did not honour the erasure/objection request and had no effective deletion procedures in practice. It fined the company EUR 20,000 for breaching Articles 17, 21 and 12(3) and Article 25(1) GDPR.
The Icelandic DPA (Persónuvernd) held that a public institution was, on the basis of the Icelandic Act on Public Archives, not permitted to delete the complainant's personal information.

The Austrian DPA (DSB) held that the negative PCR (SARS_CoV-2) test is to be qualified as a health data pursuant to Article(4)(15) GDPR and that the scope of protection of Article 9(2) must be taken into account as a standard in the subsequent review of lawfulness. The DPA also comes to the conclusion that in context of the current pandemic the transfer of health data relevant here can be based on the legal obligation of the respondent to also transfer negative PCR test results to the competent district administrative authority, which is laid down in § 3(1) EpiG in connection with § 1( 3) of the ordinance of the Minister of Health, Federal Law Gazette II No. 323/2020.
The Belgian DPA (APD/GBA) sets out best practices for transparency in a layered privacy policy and how to facilitate the right to object to direct marketing in the telecom sector.

The Spanish AEPD closed procedure PS/00430/2020 against Vodafone España after the company paid a fine. A data subject who had asked for deletion and had already obtained two earlier sanctions for the same conduct kept receiving invoice-availability emails from Vodafone in 2020. The initiation agreement proposed EUR 200,000 for a presumed breach of Article 6(1) GDPR. Two 20% reductions (acknowledgement of responsibility and voluntary payment) brought it to EUR 120,000, which the company paid on 2 February 2021. The resolution terminates the procedure.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) imposed a fine of €2,000 against Ripobruna 207, S.L. (defendant) for the alleged violation of Article 5(1)(c) GDPR for the unauthorised use of two video surveillance cameras that also recorded parts of the public road without any justified cause. The original fine of €2,000 was reduced for voluntary payment to €1,600.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) found that the data processor, Vamavi Phone SL, had violated Article 48(1) LGT, Article 21 GDPR in link with Article 23 LOPDGDD and Article 28 GDPR by making a commercial call on behalf of Vodafone España, SAU to a data subject registered on the Robinson List. Vamavi paid a fine of €24,000 (reduced from €40,000).
The Dutch DPA fined a hospital € 440,000 for violating Article 32(1) of the GDPR by failing to comply with the requirement of two-factor authentication and regular review of access log files.

The National School of Judiciary and Public Prosecution notified a personal data breach after a copy of its training platform user database, created during a test migration in February 2020, was posted publicly online in April 2020. The data of about 50,000 judicial staff and others was affected. The Polish DPA found that the School had not applied adequate security measures, had not tested their effectiveness during the migration, and had entrusted processing to a hosting company under a processing agreement that did not meet Article 28(3). It imposed the statutory maximum fine of PLN 100,000 on the School and discontinued the proceedings in all other respects, including those against the processor for the remaining alleged breaches.

After press reports, the Italian DPA investigated the Ministry of Economic Development, which had published online a list of over 5,000 'qualified managers' with names, tax codes, emails and full CVs, freely downloadable. The Garante found the publication lacked a suitable legal basis, since a directorial decree is not a regulation and was not provided for by the primary law. It also found the Ministry appointed its data protection officer and notified the contact details late. The Garante fined the Ministry EUR 75,000, ordered publication of the decision and noted it in its internal register.

A hospital foundation notified a personal data breach: because two patients had the same name, a postal package containing one patient's medical report was sent to a homonymous third party. The Garante found this was a disclosure of health data without a legal basis, breaching the lawfulness and confidentiality principles and Article 9. No further corrective measures were needed because the foundation had already contacted the patients, sent the correct documents and reviewed its processes. It imposed a fine of EUR 5,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

Permits for limited traffic zones (ZTL) in Rome carried a QR code that anyone could read with a generic mobile app, giving access to the names of permit holders and users and vehicle plates. By changing a numeric parameter in the verification web address, other permits could be viewed without any authentication. The Garante found breaches of the basic principles, the lack of a legal basis, the absence of a processor contract with the hosting provider Atac, and inadequate security. It fined Roma Capitale EUR 350,000, ordered corrective authentication measures within 30 days and ordered publication of the decision.

Roma Servizi, processor for Roma Capitale, issued paper ZTL (limited traffic zone) permits with QR codes that anyone could decode with a generic app to reach the permit holder's and user's personal data. The online verification service had no authentication, and changing a numeric ID in the URL exposed other permits. The Garante found a breach of Article 32 GDPR, fined the company EUR 60,000, ordered stronger authentication (password quality, brute-force protection) within 30 days, and ordered publication of the decision.

A hospital group notified a personal data breach after a patient found, in the digital copy of her own medical record, lab reports belonging to 7 other patients. The Garante found the processing unlawful, in breach of the principles of lawfulness and integrity/confidentiality, Article 9 and Article 32 GDPR, and Article 75 of the Italian Code. No corrective measures were ordered because the conduct had ceased and the documents were returned. It fined the hospital EUR 45,000 and ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website.

The Romanian DPA (ANSPDCP) conducted an investigation into ING Bank N.V. Amsterdam – Bucharest Branch, following a personal data breach notification, and found that the controller sent files containing outdated information to a contractual partner, through a mandated company.
The Swedish DPA (IMY) fined the Swedish Police Authority €248,218 for unlawful use of the facial recognition app Clearview AI, in violation of several paragraphs as per the Swedish Criminal Data Act.
The Slovenian DPA decided that car registration plates may be personal data.

The Belgian DPA (APD/GBA) ordered an employer to delete the HR evaluation data on its employees. The decision comes after a complaint filed by an employee concerning an access request on his emails, IT logs and other films processed by the employer.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) imposed a fine of €5,000 on Predase Servicios Integrales SL for infringing Article 13 GDPR. PSI did not have a privacy policy, nor any information on processing in the contact section of its webpage (which required the provision of personal data).

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) imposed a fine of €5,000 on the owner of a property that he rented out. The defendant had placed a video camera inside the rented property which went beyond filming the entrance as he claimed. This breached Article 5(1)(c) GDPR.

The Dutch DPA fined an unnamed orthodontic practice €12,000 for failing to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to secure personal data, including that belonging to children, on its website.

A former employee complained that Cyberbook AS had switched on automatic forwarding of their personal mailbox at the company. The forwarding went on for several months and the person was never told. The Norwegian Data Protection Authority found that this broke the regulations on employers' access to email, and also the GDPR requirements on legal basis, information, handling the employee's objection, and deletion. It ordered the company to set up written routines for access to current and former employees' mailboxes and to pay a NOK 200,000 fine.

A customer asked Iberdrola Clientes in November 2016 to cancel her personal data and gave a new notification address after moving out of the supplied property. Iberdrola kept sending payment demands to the old supply address, where the letters were returned, and her data were reported to the ASNEF debtor file. Iberdrola also kept using the old address after it had been told of the change, and did not act on the cancellation request. The AEPD fined the company EUR 50,000 for breaching the accuracy principle in Article 5(1)(d) GDPR and EUR 50,000 for breaching Article 17 GDPR, a total of EUR 100,000.

Upon a request for prior consultation under Article 36(1) GDPR, the Austrian DPA held that a high risk found in a data protection impact assessment was sufficiently mitigated by measures proposed by the controller.

Personvernnemda (PVN) holds that the posting of personal data related to a credit rating and bankruptcy case for a news article falls under the exemption for journalistic activities. PVN highlights that the wording of the national implementation of the exemption is too broad and must include a balancing of proportionality.

Roma Capitale published in full, on its online official notice board, a school canteen debt notice containing personal data of a 9-year-old child and the mother. It did so to notify a homeless person with a conventional address, relying on a city executive resolution. The Garante found a breach of lawfulness and minimisation principles and the lack of a proper legal basis for online dissemination, since a municipal resolution is not a law or regulation. It fined the city EUR 10,000 and ordered it to bring notifications to homeless residents into line with state law, which never provides for publishing the whole act.

A mother complained that a company distributing gift packs to (expectant) mothers passed on her data to third-party partners for direct marketing, and that she was still contacted after objecting. After an Inspection Service investigation, the Litigation Chamber found that the company breached the GDPR on principles, lawful basis and consent, information, accountability, data protection by design and processor arrangements. It ordered the company to bring its processing into line within six months and imposed a fine of EUR 50,000. The Chamber refused to reduce the fine despite the company's COVID-19 financial difficulties, and decided to publish the decision with the company's identity.

A hospital nurse in the gynaecology ward of a Romagna health authority hospital phoned a patient after discharge using an old number from the records, not the one the patient had given for this stay, and spoke to the patient's husband, revealing the ward. The patient had expressly refused to let third parties know about her health, and had undergone a voluntary termination of pregnancy. The Garante found that the authority's technical and organisational measures were inadequate and that the processing breached Articles 5(1)(a), (d), (f), 9 and 32(1)(b) GDPR. It imposed a fine of EUR 50,000 and ordered publication of the decision, with no further corrective measures since the conduct had ceased and the authority had put new measures in place.

A university hospital in Parma notified the Garante of two data breaches in which medical records handed to a patient's parents and to a deceased patient's heir contained test reports belonging to other patients. The Garante merged the proceedings and found that placing other patients' health data in the records disclosed it to unauthorised persons without a legal basis, breaching Articles 5(1)(f) and 9 GDPR. No corrective measures were ordered because the conduct had ceased and the hospital had taken remedial steps. It imposed a single fine of EUR 10,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

The Italian DPA (Garante per la protezione dei dati personali) reprimanded Barclays for an excessive retention of the complainants’ personal data in a credit information system (CIS) recognising that it was an isolated and bona fide mistake.

The Information Commissioner's Office (UK) has issued a fine to a security systems company that received 94 complaints because of unsolicited direct marketing calls violating the Data Protection Act (DPA) and the Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations (PECR).

The Danish DPA (Datatilsynet) found that a university's use of an online proctoring service to identify exam candidates, supervise the online test and prevent cheating, was in line with the GDPR and national legislation.

A prepaid mobile customer complained that his phone number was assigned to a third party for four days, his SIM card was deactivated, and the third party could have accessed his calls and linked accounts. The Litigation Chamber found that the provider had not taken enough precautions in identifying and verifying prepaid customers, and had not notified the breach to the authority or the data subject. It imposed a EUR 25,000 fine and ordered the provider to bring its processing into compliance within three months. A note at the top states the decision was later repealed by decision 61/2021 of 19 May 2021.
The Italian DPA provisionally orders TikTok to restrict processing of personal data of persons whose age TikTok is not certain of.
The Swedish DPA held that a controller has violated article 12(3) GDPR, because, although they complied with an erasure request, they did not subsequently notify the data subject.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) imposed a fine of €50,000 on Alterna Operador Integral SL (Flip Energy) for processing a data subject's personal data without a legal basis (Article 6(1) GDPR). Flip Energy had switched switched the data subject over from the energy provider Naturgy to Flip Energy without obtaining consent or a contract for doing so.

The complainant held several mobile lines with the controller, one used by her son. Third parties impersonating her had the ownership of one line transferred to a third party without any identity check, and a replacement SIM was then issued in a shop. The controller admitted the data had been misused but argued that the fault lay with the impersonator and that its verification procedure was adequate. The AEPD rejected this, finding no proof of the diligence required by the lawfulness principle, and imposed a fine of EUR 75,000 for infringing Article 6(1) GDPR.

The controller sent unsolicited offers through the Czech data box system to 4,238 natural persons between 2 November and 3 December 2020, without any legal basis and without giving the information required by Article 14. The Office found two offences (breach of Article 6(1) and of Article 14 GDPR). Following the accused's objection to an earlier penalty order, which was cancelled, it imposed a single fine of CZK 285,000 under the absorption principle, plus CZK 1,000 costs. Aggravating factors were the abuse of data boxes during the state of emergency, the large number of people affected and the multiple breaches.

The controller sent unsolicited offers through the Czech data-box system to 23,302 natural persons between 2 November and 3 December 2020, during a state of emergency when data-box messages were free. It had no legal basis under Article 6(1) and did not give the Article 14 information. The Office found two offences and, applying the absorption principle, imposed a single fine of CZK 666,000 plus CZK 1,000 costs. The earlier penalty order was cancelled after the controller objected, and the controller made no statement in the proceedings.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) imposed a €2000 fine on The Washpoint SL for failing to provide a Privacy Policy on their website (Article 13 GDPR) and for the absence of a reject button on the second layer of their Cookie Policy (Article 22(2) LSSI).

The Polish DPA imposed a fine of €5000 on a company for failing to comply with the obligation to cooperate with the supervisory authority and not providing it with all information necessary to fulfil its tasks in the course of the proceedings.

The Finnish DPA ordered the data processor, the City of Helsinki, to align its data processing practice related to the criminal background check of applicants seeking to volunteer as a support person for children and young persons.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) held that a consumers and users association (ASOCAPAC) breached Article 22(2) LSSI. The first layer of the cookie banner and the cookie policy on their website did not contain sufficient information and a "refuse all cookies" option was missing.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) imposed a €1000 fine on a beauty salon for breaching Article 17 GDPR and Article 21 LSSI. The salon sent a marketing SMS to a client months after confirming that they had deleted the client's personal data.

The Latvian DPA (Datu valsts inspekcija) imposed a fine of €65,000 on SIA “Lursoft IT" for breaching Articles 5(1)(a), (b), (c) and 6(1) GDPR. Lursoft published personal data from the "Insolvency Register" as well as personal data that is to be submitted to the "Register of Enterprises" on its website.

The Norwegian DPA fined a company €38,800 for unlawfully disclosing personal data from a surveillance footage, thus breaching Article 5(1)(a) GDPR and Article 6. The company appealed to the Norwegian Privacy Appeals Board, who first removed the fine in its entirety, then awarded the controller €6,959 to cover their legal costs.

ARPAC, a regional environmental agency, notified the Garante of the theft of an external hard disk from its offices. The disk held identity documents, tax documents, payslips and refund files and was connected to a server in a room any employee could enter. The backup had failed, so most data was permanently lost. The Garante found that ARPAC had no adequate security measures (no working backup or restoration, no pseudonymisation or encryption, no regular testing). It fined ARPAC EUR 8,000 for breaching Articles 5(1)(f) and 32 and ordered publication of the decision.

A data subject asked the clinic on 19 September 2019 for access under Article 15 to her own data and to data about her two minor daughters. The clinic answered only after the Garante's office intervened, 62 days after the request. The clinic blamed a hardware failure that led to a PC replacement. The Garante found a breach of Article 12(3) in relation to Article 15, treated the delay as negligent rather than intentional, noted the clinic's cooperation and lack of relevant prior breaches, and imposed a fine of EUR 2,000 with publication of the decision on its website.

The Bologna health authority notified a personal data breach: because of a manual error by a technician of its supplier, hospital discharge letters with therapies of oncology patients were wrongly loaded into 182 electronic health records (49 active). Only 14 holders opened their record in the period, and two patients certainly saw other people's documents. The documents were deleted after about six hours. The Garante found a breach of Articles 5(1)(f) and 9 GDPR and imposed a fine of EUR 18,000, plus publication of the decision. No corrective measures were ordered because the conduct had ceased.

The Italian DPA investigated Regione Lazio's regional health-booking call centre service (ReCUP), run by an external cooperative. The Region never validly appointed the cooperative as data processor; the earlier appointments were found to have no effect, and a proper Article 28 appointment was only made in January 2019. The Garante found the processing unlawful from 1999 to January 2019, in breach of Articles 5(2)(a) and 28 GDPR. It fined the Region EUR 75,000 and ordered publication of the decision, but adopted no corrective measures since the conduct had ended.

The Belgian DPA (APD/GBA) held that sending a newsletter to the parents of school children with all email addresses visible in CC was a breach of the Article 5(1)(b), as this was not within the reasonable expectations of the parents to have their email address distributed. Furthermore, the school cannot rely on legitimate interest (Article 6(1)(f)) as other measures exist to not share the contact details with the other parents (BCC) and the parents do not expect their personal data from being further processed. As such, the school does not comply with their responsibilities as controller nor does uphold the principles of data protection by design and default (Articles 24 and 25).
The Spanish DPA (AEDP) accepted a complaint against 'Associació Catalana per la Participació Política' as the organisation failed to respond to a citizen's request for suppression (Article 17 GDPR).

The French DPA (CNIL) ordered the Ministry of Interior to cease the use of drones equipped with cameras by police forces. The Ministry violated its obligations to process personal data only where authorised by a specific legal provision and to conduct a privacy impact assessment.
The Cyprus Data Protection Authority (Επίτροπος Δεδομένων Προσωπικού Χαρακτήρα) found that consent is not an appropriate legal basis for processing employees' personal health data.

The Norwegian DPA fined a company €38,800 (NOK 400,000) for enabling automatic forwarding of an employee's emails during a sick leave, without informing the employee or accepting her objection. The company appealed the fine and although the Privacy Appeals Board (Personvernnemnda) agreed with the DPA that the fine was correct, they reduced it to NOK 250,000 only because of the DPA's long case processing time.

A performing artist complained that a company and its manager ran a Facebook fan page carrying her full name without her consent, and ignored her requests to hand over control and to stop. After an earlier interim decision (14/2020) that was not complied with, the Litigation Chamber examined the case on the merits. It dismissed the complaint against the manager, who was not a controller, and warned the company on data portability, a request that had become moot because Facebook transferred the admin rights to the complainant. It found the company had no lawful basis for the processing (Art. 6(1)) and failed to act on the objection and communicate properly (Art. 21(1) with 12(3)), and fined it EUR 10,000.
The Polish DPA (Urząd Ochrony Danych Osobowych) imposed an administrative fine of over PLN 136,000 (approx. €30,000) on an energy sector company for failing to report a data protection breach.

The Polish DPA (UODO) reprimanded a company for using outdated software, ineffective safeguards for the IT system and the failure to adequately test, measure and evaluate the effectiveness of technical and organizational measures to ensure the security of personal data processed in the IT systems.

The Belgian DPA (APD/GBA) decided, in an interlocutory decision, on the language to be used in a procedure concerning GDPR complaints filed by complainants in various Member States against IAB Europe. The DPA chose French, as English is not a national language in Belgium and the defendant, who does not speak Dutch, requested French as the procedural language.

The Austrian DPA (Datenschutzbehörde) held that a respondent may subsequently remedy the alleged infringement by complying with the complainant's requests until the conclusion of the proceedings before the data protection authority. Furthermore, the principle of the place of market inherent in the GDPR implies that information and notifications must in principle be translated into the languages of those countries in which the entrepreneur offers the services in question, taking into account the nationality or place of residence of the data subject.

The Norwegian DPA (Datatilsynet) fined Gveik AS NOK 75,000 (€7,200) for subjecting the complainant to a credit rating without a legal basis under Article 6(1)(f) GDPR and for not adhering to the accountability principle as per Article 5(2). The DPA also requires that the company implement internal controls of their credit rating process as per Article 24.

The Polish DPA imposed a fine of €5,500 on the Silesian Medical University for failing to notify both the DPA and data subjects about the data breach which had occurred in connection with exams conducted on an e-learning platform.

A former employee of a medical business copied the personal data of 100 patients to market his own services, and the business notified the breach to UODO but chose not to inform the patients despite rating the risk as high. UODO ordered it in February 2020 to notify the patients with the content required by Article 34(2). The business sent incomplete notices and failed to prove it had complied, and ignored guidance from UODO staff. UODO therefore fined it PLN 85,588 (the equivalent of EUR 20,000) under Article 83(6) for not complying with a corrective order.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) issued a warning to the Town Hall of Tobar for publicly posting a list with the personal data of citizens on jury duty on a street. The DPA considered this a breach of Article 5(1)(f) GDPR.

The Romanian DPA (ANSPDCP) imposed a €3000 fine on ING Bank N.V. Amsterdam – Bucharest Branch for unlawfully processing the personal data of a natural person after the conclusion of their contractual relationship.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) sanctioned Vodafone España, S.A.U. for non-compliance with general data processing principles. The initial proposed fine was €90,000 however, it was reduced to €54,000 for recognition of responsibility and making an early payment of the fine.

The President of the Polish Office for Personal Data Protection (UODO) imposed a fine of around €18,900 on an insurance company for failing to notify a personal data breach to the DPA without undue delay and for failing to notify a personal data breach without undue delay to data subjects.

The Belgian DPA (APD/GBA) held that disclosure of personal data cannot be a condition for an individual to access public information. The DPA therefore reprimanded the Federal Public Service of Finance for requiring citizens to use a Microsoft account to access the Fisconetplus portal of the Federal Public Service of Finance in order to complete their tax declaration.

A complainant filed a complaint against a street-parking company (first respondent) and a bailiff's office collecting its debts (second respondent). The Litigation Chamber found breaches of transparency/information duties, access rights, lawful basis, data minimisation and accountability. It reprimanded both respondents, issued compliance orders, and fined the parking company EUR 50,000 and the bailiff's office EUR 15,000. A note at the top says the Market Court annulled the whole decision on 26 May 2021, though later case law again allowed fines for a first infringement.

A complainant filed a complaint against a street-parking company and the bailiff's office that collected its debts. The Litigation Chamber found both breached transparency and information duties, lawfulness, data minimisation and accountability rules. It reprimanded both and ordered each to bring its practices into compliance. It fined the parking company EUR 50,000 and the bailiff's office EUR 15,000. The Market Court later annulled the whole decision, mainly because of the fine.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) initiated a sanctioning procedure against the utility company, Iberdrola Clientes, S.A.U for infringing Article 21 GDPR, Article 48(1)(b) LGT, and Article 23(4) LOPDGDD. The initial proposed fine was €10000 however, it was reduced to €6000, for recognition of responsibility and early payment of the fine.
The Romanian DPA (ANSPDCP) imposed an approximately €2000 fine on SC C&V Water Control SA for failing to provide information to the DPA during the investigation.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) imposed a fine of €60000 (reduced to €36000) on Banco Bilbao Vizcaya Argentaria, SA. (BBVA) for processing personal data without the accuracy required according to Article 5(1)(d) GDPR.
The Dutch DPA fined a Canada-based controller €525,000 for not appointing an EU representative despite offering services to individuals within the EU.

An natural person received a warning from the Spanish DPA (AEPD) for tweeting a photo of a bill where the name, surname, fiscal ID and bank account of a restaurant owner was visible. This constituted a breach of Article 5(1)(a) GDPR.

The respondent sent unsolicited offers through the data boxes of natural persons from 2 November to 3 December 2020, reaching 376 persons, during the state of emergency when sending data messages was free. It had no legal basis for processing and did not give the information required by Article 14. The Czech authority found two offences by penalty order and imposed one fine of CZK 208,000 for the more serious offence (Article 6(1)), applying the absorption principle.

The Czech DPA issued a penalty order against a company that, from 2 November to 3 December 2020, sent unsolicited offers through the data boxes of 1,743 natural persons without any legal basis and without giving the Article 14 information. It found breaches of Article 6(1) and Article 14 GDPR. Applying the absorption principle, it imposed a single fine of CZK 235,000, based on the more serious unlawful-processing offence. Aggravating factors were the abuse of free data boxes during the state of emergency, the large number of people affected and the breach of several obligations.

The Czech DPA issued a penalty order against a legal person that sent unsolicited offers through the data boxes of 2,566 natural persons between 2 November and 3 December 2020. It had no legal basis for processing and did not give the Article 14 information. The authority found two offences and, applying the absorption principle, imposed a single fine of CZK 251,000. Aggravating factors included the abuse of free data box messaging during the state of emergency and the large number of people affected.

The Czech DPA issued a penalty order against a company that sent unsolicited commercial offers through the data boxes of natural persons between 2 November and 3 December 2020. It had no legal basis for processing and did not provide the Article 14 information. The Ministry of the Interior reported that 6,119 natural persons were contacted. The company was fined CZK 322,000 under the absorption principle, with the unlawful processing treated as the most serious offence.

The Czech DPA issued a penalty order against a controller that, from 2 November to 3 December 2020, sent unsolicited offers through the data boxes of individuals, contacting 4,238 natural persons. It had no legal basis for this under Article 6(1) and did not give the Article 14 information. The two offences were handled together and a single fine of CZK 285,000 was imposed. The authority treated the conduct as especially harmful because it took place during the state of emergency, when sending data messages was free.

The Czech DPA issued a penalty order against an association that, between 2 November and 3 December 2020, sent unsolicited offers to 23,302 natural persons through their official data boxes. It had no legal basis for processing their data and gave them none of the Article 14 information. The Office found two offences, applied the absorption principle, and imposed a single fine of CZK 666,000. The order can be challenged by an objection within 8 days.

The Czech DPA issued a penalty order against a legal person that sent unsolicited offers through the data boxes of natural persons between 2 November and 3 December 2020, reaching 1,035 individuals. It had no legal basis for processing and did not give the information required by Article 14. The two offences were handled together and a single fine of CZK 221,000 was imposed under the absorption principle, based on the more serious unlawful-processing offence. The conduct was treated as aggravated because it took place during the state of emergency, when data box messages were free, and involved a large number of people.

The Czech DPA issued a penalty order against a company that, from 2 November to 3 December 2020, sent unsolicited offers to individuals' official data boxes without any legal basis. It contacted 1,060 natural persons and did not give them the Article 14 information. The authority found breaches of Article 6(1) and Article 14 GDPR and, applying the absorption principle, imposed one fine of CZK 221,000 under Article 83(5). The fine was aggravated by the abuse of free data box messaging during the state of emergency, the large number of people affected and the multiple breaches.

The Czech DPA issued a penalty order against a company that sent unsolicited offers through the data boxes of natural persons between 2 November and 3 December 2020. According to the Ministry of the Interior, it contacted 80 natural persons this way. The Office found that it had no legal basis for processing (Art. 6(1)) and did not give the information required by Art. 14. It imposed a single fine of CZK 202,000, applying the absorption principle, based on the more serious offence (unlawful processing).

The Slovenian DPA (IP) issued an advisory opinion about the use of personal data for advertising purposes on Facebook and joint controllership. It underlined that each controller needs a legal basis for processing personal data.
